clinicalPearls: A fibroinflammatory disorder whose hallmark is a tendency to form tumefactive (mass-like) lesions that frequently mimic malignancy; initial misdiagnosis as cancer is extremely common.

Protean and multisystem: can affect virtually any organ, with predilection for pancreas, biliary tree, major salivary glands (submandibular, parotid), periorbital/lacrimal tissues, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, and retroperitoneum; meninges, aorta, prostate, thyroid, pericardium, and skin are also described.
Regarded as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can target arteries and veins of any size, with venous involvement (obliterative phlebitis) being a particular hallmark.

Typical patient is a middle-aged to elderly man (male-to-female ratio about 2:1), contrasting with classic autoimmune diseases that favor young women; head-and-neck (orbit, lacrimal, salivary) disease has a sex ratio closer to 1:1.
Usually presents subacutely; most patients lack fever or marked C-reactive protein elevation even with multiorgan disease. Substantial weight loss can occur, often from exocrine pancreatic failure.
Mikulicz's disease (lacrimal, parotid, and submandibular gland enlargement), once thought to be a Sjogren's subset, is one of the most common presentations of IgG4-RD.
Allergic features are common: atopy, eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, sinusitis, and modest peripheral eosinophilia.

Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis classically shows a diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with loss of normal lobularity; 20-50% of patients present with acute glucose intolerance and a pancreatic mass mimicking adenocarcinoma.
Diagnosis requires correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings; pathology alone is never sufficient, and biopsy is often done mainly to exclude malignancy.

Renal involvement (tubulointerstitial nephritis) is strongly associated with hypocomplementemia; membranous glomerulonephropathy is a less common renal manifestation that must be distinguished from idiopathic disease.
Clinical course is variable: disease may relapse and remit within a given organ, accumulate new organ involvement over time, or be found incidentally on imaging.
Disease can evolve over months, years, or even decades before an organ becomes symptomatic enough to prompt medical attention.
harrison.pathophysiology: IgG4-RD is characterized by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, a distinctive storiform (woven-mat / basket-weave) pattern of fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis reflecting vascular tropism, and a mild-to-moderate tissue eosinophilia. The infiltrate combines B cells (organized in germinal centers, with IgG4+ CD19/CD138 plasma cells radiating outward) and a more diffusely distributed, predominant population of CD4+ T cells. Despite the disease's name, the IgG4 molecule itself is not thought to directly drive injury in most organs: IgG4 undergoes Fab-arm exchange, binds antigen weakly, and has low affinity for Fc receptors and C1q, making it a generally noninflammatory immunoglobulin that may even play a counterregulatory role. A unique oligoclonally expanded CD4+ cytotoxic T cell, abundant at tissue sites, secretes interferon-gamma, TGF-beta, and interleukin-1 (driving storiform fibrosis) as well as perforin, granzymes A/B, and granulysin (mediating cytotoxicity), and appears to be a major disease driver. Oligoclonal plasmablast expansions in blood, with continuous B-cell/plasmablast antigen presentation, are thought to support these profibrotic, tissue-injuring CD4+ cytotoxic T cells.
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (mimicked by type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma (mimicked by IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis)
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (when destructive sinus/middle-ear/nasopharyngeal lesions occur)
Lymphoma and other causes of lymphadenopathy or pseudotumor
Riedel's thyroiditis and fibrosing variant of Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Orbital pseudotumor / orbital myositis from other causes
nonInfectiousMimics: Malignancy (carcinoma, lymphoma) presenting as a tumefactive mass
Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis and inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm
additionalInvestigations: Serum IgG4 concentration (commonly elevated, but normal in ~30% of histologically proven cases; usually measured by nephelometry).

Awareness of the prozone effect: very high serum IgG4 can yield spuriously low/normal nephelometric values, correctable by serum dilution; failure to detect dramatic elevations misses the subset at greatest risk for multiorgan disease and end-organ injury.
Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) to map multiorgan involvement and detect subclinical or incidental disease.
MRI of brain/orbits for pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement or enlarged extraocular muscles in CNS/orbital disease.
Tissue biopsy with immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 and IgG, quantifying IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field and the IgG4:total IgG ratio.
Complement levels (hypocomplementemia associated with renal/tubulointerstitial involvement).
Serial serum IgG4 monitoring after treatment to detect rising levels signaling possible flare.
redFlags: New tumefactive mass mimicking cancer in pancreas, salivary gland, orbit, lung, or other organ.
Obstructive jaundice from pancreatic or biliary involvement (undiagnosed/undertreated sclerosing cholangitis can lead to hepatic failure within months).
Ureteral entrapment, hydronephrosis, postobstructive uropathy, and renal atrophy from retroperitoneal fibrosis.
Aortic involvement causing aneurysm or dissection.
Anterior pituitary hormone deficiency and/or central diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic-pituitary involvement.
Spinal cord compression, cranial nerve palsies, or radiculopathy from hypertrophic pachymeningitis.
Destructive bone lesions of sinuses, head, and middle ear mimicking granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Persistently rising serum IgG4 concentrations signaling risk of clinical flare and serious organ involvement.
Coronary arteritis (wall thickening, periarterial encasement, stenosis, calcification, aneurysm/ectasia) in longstanding disease with high IgG4 and biomarker levels.
harrison.prognosis: Course is generally subacute but can cause major morbidity and organ failure. Aggressive disease may rapidly produce end-stage liver disease, permanent pancreatic exocrine and endocrine (diabetes) impairment, renal atrophy, aortic dissection or aneurysm, and destructive sinonasal lesions. Some manifestations (e.g., IgG4-related lymphadenopathy) can remain indolent and asymptomatic for years. Even with apparently effective immunosuppression, renal atrophy is a frequent sequel to tubulointerstitial nephritis, and end-organ fibrotic damage may be irreversible if diagnosis is delayed. Relapses are common, including in patients with persistently normal IgG4 levels.
pitfalls: Treating the disease as purely IgG4-antibody-mediated; the IgG4 molecule is largely noninflammatory and may be counterregulatory rather than a primary driver.

Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgG4 is normal: ~30% of histologically proven cases have normal levels, and retroperitoneal fibrosis (often advanced/fibrotic at presentation) frequently shows normal IgG4.
Missing markedly elevated IgG4 because of the prozone effect on nephelometry; suspect this when results are normal despite strong clinical features and re-test with dilution.
Relying on pathology alone for diagnosis; histopathology, while characteristic, is essentially never diagnostic by itself and must be interpreted with clinical, serologic, and radiologic data.
Mistaking tumefactive lesions for malignancy and proceeding to major resections (e.g., Whipple procedure, thyroidectomy) before the correct diagnosis is recognized.

Histologic features such as intense neutrophilic infiltration, leukocytoclasis, granulomatous inflammation, multinucleated giant cells, or fibrinoid necrosis are uncommon in IgG4-RD and argue against the diagnosis.
Assuming serum IgG4 reliably tracks disease activity; correlations are imperfect, levels often do not fully normalize, and remissions can occur with persistently elevated levels.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal numeric severity score is given. Practical stratification distinguishes vital/organ-threatening involvement (e.g., pancreas, biliary tree/liver, kidneys, aorta, sinonasal destruction, pituitary, meninges) requiring prompt treatment from indolent manifestations (e.g., asymptomatic lymphadenopathy) amenable to watchful waiting with close monitoring; classification of disease itself relies on correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings (ACR/EULAR classification criteria are referenced).
management: Confirm the diagnosis histologically to exclude malignancy before committing to immunosuppression, given the tumefactive mimicry
Induce remission with glucocorticoids as first-line therapy for symptomatic or organ-threatening disease
Use rituximab-based B-cell depletion for induction in aggressive disease and for relapse or steroid intolerance, often with a steroid-sparing agent
Manage organ-specific sequelae such as pancreatic exocrine insufficiency with enzyme replacement, resulting diabetes with insulin, and biliary obstruction with drainage
Monitor for the frequent relapses with serial imaging, serum IgG4 and organ-function testing
Consider watchful waiting for asymptomatic, non-organ-threatening disease
Coordinate multidisciplinary care given the multisystem distribution
